fixes.title: State and Strategy differ by intent
fixes.body: State models the object's own lifecycle mode: the same call behaves differently as the order moves between states, and the context or states own the transitions. Strategy is an interchangeable algorithm for one step, chosen from outside as policy, so the class diagram alone cannot tell them apart.

fixes.title: Static singletons and captive DbContext dependencies
fixes.body: `RateLimitConfig.Instance` hides a dependency and shares global state across tests, so register a plain class with `AddSingleton` and inject it through the constructor. A singleton cache that holds a scoped `DbContext` is a captive dependency; it also needs a thread-safe, size-bounded store. Create a scope for each load (`IServiceScopeFactory`) or make the cache scoped.

fixes.title: Bridge splits two independently growing dimensions
fixes.body: When operations and providers both grow, an operation hierarchy holds an `IPaymentGateway` and delegates to it. A new provider then needs one new gateway, and a new operation needs one new class, instead of a new method for every provider × operation pair. Injecting one gateway varies only the provider dimension, which is ordinary Strategy or polymorphism.

cards.front: Why is Bridge more than injecting one `IPaymentGateway` through DI, and what is one limit of Bridge?
cards.back: DI with one interface varies only one dimension, the provider. Bridge adds a second hierarchy on the abstraction side (operations such as Charge or PartialRefund) that holds the gateway and delegates to it. A new provider is one gateway class, and a new operation is one operation class. Shared retry and logging can live in the abstraction. Limit: a genuinely new primitive changes the gateway interface and every provider. Bridge is also premature when only one dimension varies.

cards.front: An `AddSingleton` cache takes a scoped EF Core `DbContext` and stores entries in a plain `Dictionary`. Name three problems and their fixes.
cards.back: 1) Captive dependency: the scoped `DbContext` outlives its scope, and scope validation rejects this. Fix: create and dispose a scope per load with `IServiceScopeFactory`, or make the cache scoped. 2) Thread safety: concurrent requests share one `Dictionary`. Fix: use `ConcurrentDictionary` or a lock. 3) Unbounded memory: the cache lives as long as the provider. Fix: add a size or expiry bound, or use `IMemoryCache`.

cards.front: What are the Observer pitfalls with async server subscribers that must run in order, and with C# event leaks in a desktop UI?
cards.back: Server: C# events are synchronous and lead to `async void`, so use a Task-returning observer interface. Define a failure policy (fail the operation, isolate or aggregate). Make ordering explicit with an awaited sequential loop or a workflow; never rely on subscription order or `Task.WhenAll`. UI: the publisher's delegate list references each subscriber, so a long-lived view model keeps closed views alive. Fix: unsubscribe with `-=` using the same delegate when the view closes; use weak events only as a fallback. Observer is overkill for one required dependent or a small fixed set; use a direct call.

cards.front: GRASP: where do `Order` total, persistence and email go, and why?
cards.back: Total goes on `Order` (Information Expert): it owns the line items and the invariant, so callers stop reaching into its internals. Persistence goes in a repository and email in an email gateway (Pure Fabrication), keeping I/O out of the domain object (Low Coupling, High Cohesion). Information Expert names a strong candidate, not an automatic winner: the principles conflict, and the dominant pressure decides.

cards.front: Template Method vs Strategy: what favors Strategy for report formatting?
cards.back: Strategy is a composed object passed to the context. It can be picked per request and reused by any class without inheriting from the base, so it does not use up the single base-class slot. Template Method fixes the variant in a subclass, set per object and coupled to the hook order. It fits a stable, base-owned workflow whose variants differ only in a few hooks.

cards.front: Adapter, Decorator, Proxy, Facade: which wrapper controls whether, when or how a call reaches the real object?
cards.back: Proxy: same interface as the real object, used for lazy loading, caching or authorization. Decorator has the same interface and adds stackable responsibilities. Adapter translates to an interface the client expects. Facade gives a simpler new interface over a whole subsystem, not a single wrapped object.
